intro: You are Alan Turing, a mathematician with a stubborn habit of asking what can be computed at all. Content note: this life ends with persecution under an unjust law and an early death; the text stays factual and non-graphic.

office.why: Law: a 1952 conviction for being gay ended his security clearance and his career.

tunnel.why: Secrecy: the Official Secrets Act forced him to stay silent about his work.

ladder.why: School: Sherborne wanted Latin, not mathematics.

quiet.why: Study and thought: Cambridge gave him time to work out what computing means.

sprint.why: Running: he ran a marathon in 2h46 and trained with a club.

advantage.title: Cutting to the core
advantage.text: His 1936 paper reduced a huge question to a precise one. Twice, one wrong answer is removed before you choose.

life.title: London, 1912
life.text: Alan is born on 23 June 1912. His parents work for the British administration in India, so he grows up with foster families in England and then at boarding school.

life.title: A school that wanted Latin
life.text: At Sherborne School teachers care about Latin, sport and neat handwriting. Alan cares about science and numbers, and is criticised for his untidy work and for not fitting the school's idea of a good pupil.

life.title: Christopher
life.text: Alan's close friend Christopher Morcom shares his love of science. Christopher dies of an illness at 18. Alan is devastated and keeps pursuing science, partly in his friend's memory.

life.title: King's College, Cambridge
life.text: Alan studies mathematics at Cambridge and is elected a fellow of King's College at 22, an honour for young researchers. There, people value how he thinks.

life.title: The paper of 1936
life.text: In 1936 Alan publishes a paper that describes an imaginary machine able to carry out any calculation, given the right instructions. It lays the theoretical groundwork for every computer today.

q.q: What is the idea from his 1936 paper called?
q.x: The universal Turing machine is a theoretical model of computation. Enigma was the German cipher machine, and the Bombe was a code-breaking machine built later.

life.title: Bletchley Park
life.text: In 1939 Alan joins the secret codebreakers at Bletchley Park. He helps design the Bombe to attack the German Enigma cipher, and leads the team working on German naval messages, which protect Atlantic convoys.

life.title: A hero nobody could name
life.text: The Official Secrets Act keeps thousands of codebreakers silent for decades. Alan gets only a modest honour, an OBE in 1946, and the public does not learn what he did until long after.

life.title: Running to think
life.text: After the war Alan runs for the Walton Athletic Club and sometimes runs to meetings. His marathon times are close to Olympic level, and running gives him a way to clear his head.

life.title: Can machines think?
life.text: At the University of Manchester he works on some of the first stored-program computers. In 1950 he asks "Can machines think?" and proposes a test with a human judge.

q.q: What do we call his 1950 "imitation game" today?
q.x: The Turing Test asks whether a human judge can tell a machine from a person by conversation alone. It is still discussed in AI research.

life.title: Convicted in 1952
life.text: Sex between men is a crime in Britain. After a burglary report, police learn of Alan's relationship with a man and he is convicted of "gross indecency". Instead of prison he must accept hormone treatment for a year.

life.title: Clearance withdrawn
life.text: The conviction ends his security clearance, so he can no longer advise the government on codes. Officials treat him as a risk. He keeps working on mathematics and on how living things grow patterns, increasingly isolated.

life.title: What came after
life.text: Alan dies on 7 June 1954, aged 41. Decades later Britain apologised in 2009, pardoned him in 2013 and in 2017 pardoned thousands of other men. Since 2021 he is on the Bank of England £50 note.

sources: Bletchley Park Trust; Andrew Hodges, Alan Turing: The Enigma
UK Government apology (2009), royal pardon (2013), Policing and Crime Act 2017 (the Turing law)

evidence.ev: He was convicted of 'gross indecency' under a law that made gay sex a crime; he accepted hormone treatment instead of prison.
His security clearance was withdrawn, so he lost his work for the secret service.
His wartime codebreaking at Bletchley Park was covered by the Official Secrets Act, so he could not tell anyone.
At Sherborne School the headmaster wanted classics and Latin; he preferred science.
He was elected fellow of King's College, Cambridge, and wrote 'On Computable Numbers' in 1936.
He ran a marathon in 2 hours 46 minutes and trained with Walton Athletic Club.
